strengths: Novel and well-motivated adaptation of the datamodels/data-attribution framework (originally from NLP/CV) to robot imitation learning, specifically addressing the core obstacle of expensive/dangerous real-world rollouts via a differentiable proxy objective (held-out BC loss) that enables both regression-based and metagradient-based influence estimation.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 long-horizon tasks with a large transformer/diffusion policy (Octo), and real-world experiments on heterogeneous OXE data across multiple embodiments (Franka, Tiago, Droid) and even a multi-task real-robot setting.

Thoughtful engineering contributions specific to robotics: trajectory/sub-trajectory clustering to reduce noise in influence estimates, and a practical strategy for mitigating distribution shift by mixing target data into datamodel training for real-world settings.

Strong empirical support for design choices via targeted ablations: proxy-metric vs. true-rollout correlation (Fig. 2, 11), effect of selection percentage, cluster granularity, and co-training ratio (Fig. 13), and a sanity check that simply training All-Data longer doesn't close the gap (App. C.6).

Consistent and often large improvements over multiple well-chosen baselines (SR, AR, BR, Flow, STRAP) across nearly all settings, including qualitative analyses showing DataMIL identifies task-relevant and quality-filtered data even under embodiment/domain shift (e.g., Tiago-Sink with an unseen embodiment).

Good transparency about compute cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and scope limitations in the conclusion, plus a fairly extensive and reproducible appendix (pseudocode, hyperparameters, dataset construction details).
weaknesses: The core estimation machinery (regression and metagradient-based datamodels) is largely adopted from prior work (Ilyas et al. 2022; Engstrom et al. 2025) rather than newly developed here; the paper's novelty lies primarily in the proxy-metric substitution and robotics-specific engineering (clustering, distribution-shift mitigation), which are comparatively incremental.

The proxy metric's validity (correlation between held-out BC loss and true rollout success) is only rigorously validated on a handful of MetaWorld tasks (Fig. 2 and App. C.1, 4-5 tasks total) before being extended to LIBERO and OXE; it's unclear how well this correlation holds for more complex, high-dimensional visuomotor policies or truly out-of-distribution prior data.

Computational cost remains substantial (e.g., 3-4 days on 4 A100 GPUs for OXE-scale selection), which, combined with the acknowledged sensitivity to hyperparameters like selection ratio and cluster size (which appear to require per-dataset tuning without clear principled guidance), somewhat limits practical plug-and-play applicability.
Real-world OXE evaluations are conducted with a single seed, limiting the statistical confidence of the real-robot results despite the otherwise appealing scale of experimentation.

Concurrent related work CUPID is discussed only qualitatively (no direct empirical comparison), and it is unclear how DataMIL's offline approach would fare against CUPID's online policy-gradient influence estimation in matched settings.

In LIBERO task-wise results (Table 1), DataMIL's advantage over the strongest heuristic baselines (STRAP, BR, Flow) is often modest or occasionally reversed on individual tasks, suggesting the average improvement is somewhat driven by consistency rather than uniformly dominant performance.
